name: Nahum
sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex (the Masoretic Text). It was checked against the Hebrew Minor Prophets scrolls from Qumran (4QXII, especially 4QXII-g) and Wadi Murabba‘at (MurXII, early 2nd century AD), whose text is very close to the Masoretic Text. The transcriptions used are Martin Abegg’s, as published in the ETCBC Dead Sea Scrolls dataset. It was also checked against the Septuagint, using Brenton’s public-domain English translation. Portions of Nahum also survive in the Greek Minor Prophets Scroll from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr, about the turn of the era), which is a revision of the Septuagint toward the Hebrew. Its readings could not be checked directly, so any that are cited are marked “reported.” Significant differences are footnoted; differences of spelling and damage to the scrolls are not. Poetry is printed line by line. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible: English 1:15 is Hebrew 2:1, and English 2:1–13 is Hebrew 2:2–14.

verses.text: An oracle concerning Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite.{a}

Yahweh is a jealous God and an avenger;{b}
Yahweh avenges, and is a master of wrath.
Yahweh takes vengeance on his adversaries,
and he keeps wrath for his enemies.

Yahweh is patient and mighty,
but he never lets the guilty go unpunished.
He travels in the whirlwind and the tempest,
and the clouds are the dust kicked up by his feet.

He rebukes the sea and dries it,
and all the rivers he makes dry.
Bashan languishes, and Carmel,
and the flower of Lebanon fades.

The mountains quake because of him,
and the hills melt away.
The earth heaves at his presence,
the world and all who dwell in it.

Who can stand before his indignation?
And who can rise up in the heat of his anger?
His wrath is poured out like fire,
and the rocks are torn apart by him.

Thus says Yahweh:
“Though they are at full strength and many as well,
even so they shall be cut down and pass away.
Though I have afflicted you,
I will afflict you no more.

And now I will break his yoke from off you,
and I will tear your bonds apart.”

And Yahweh has given command concerning you:
“No more of your name shall be sown;
out of the house of your gods I will cut off
the graven image and the molten image.
I will prepare your grave, for you are vile.”

notes.text: “Oracle”: Hebrew massa’, which can also mean “burden.” The name Nahum means “comfort” or “comforter.” Where Elkosh was is not known.

Hebrew El qanno’. The poem in verses 2–8 seems partly to follow the order of the Hebrew alphabet (an acrostic), though the pattern is incomplete. In the next line, “a master of wrath” is literally “a lord (ba‘al) of wrath,” meaning one full of wrath.

“Her place” refers to Nineveh. The Septuagint has “those that rise up against him,” reading the Hebrew letters differently. The next line can also be translated “and he will pursue his enemies into darkness.”
The Hebrew of this verse is obscure, and the translation is uncertain.
Hebrew beliyya‘al, “worthlessness, wickedness.” The same word is translated “the worthless one” in verse 15.
Compare Isaiah 52:7, which Romans 10:15 quotes. In Hebrew this verse is 2:1, so English 2:1–13 is Hebrew 2:2–14.

verses.text:
For Yahweh is restoring the majesty of Jacob
like the majesty of Israel,
for the emptiers have emptied them out
and destroyed their vine branches.

The gates of the rivers are opened,
and the palace melts away.

Nineveh has been like a pool of water all her days,{d}
and now they flee.
“Stand! Stand!” they cry,
but no one turns back.

Take the spoil of silver, take the spoil of gold!
For the store has no end,
wealth of every precious thing.

Emptiness, desolation, and ruin!
Hearts melt and knees give way;
anguish is in all loins,
and all their faces grow pale.

Where now is that lions’ lair,
the place where young lions fed,
where lion and lioness walked,
and cubs played unafraid?

The lion ripped up plenty for his young
and choked the kill for his mates;
he stocked his caves with victims
and his lairs with mangled meat.

notes.text: Hebrew 2:2. “One who scatters” can also be translated “a shatterer.” The Septuagint differs: “one who has been delivered from affliction has come up panting into your presence.”

Literally “and the cypresses are made to quiver.” The Septuagint has “and the horsemen shall be thrown into confusion,” reading parashim (“horsemen”) for beroshim (“cypresses”). The Hebrew word translated “steel” (peladot) is rare, and its meaning is uncertain; some take it to mean “torches.”
The Hebrew word translated “It is decided” (hutstsav) is obscure. Some older translations treat it as a name (“Huzzab”); others take it to mean the queen or a goddess’s image.
The Hebrew phrase translated “all her days” is difficult. The Septuagint has “her waters shall be as a pool of water.”

Hebrew YHWH Tseva’ot, traditionally “the LORD of hosts.” The “armies” are the forces of heaven (the angels and the stars) and sometimes the armies of Israel. The title is given as “Yahweh of Armies” throughout. In Hebrew this verse is 2:14.
Hebrew “her chariots.” The Septuagint has “your multitude.”

verses.text:
The crack of the whip and the rumble of the wheel,
the galloping horse and the bounding chariot!

Horsemen charging, the flashing sword and the glittering spear,
a multitude of slain, a mass of corpses,
dead bodies without end;
they stumble over their dead.

All for the countless harlotries of the harlot,
graceful and charming, a mistress of sorceries,
who sells nations by her harlotries
and peoples by her sorceries.

“I am your enemy,” announces Yahweh of Armies,
“and I will pull your skirts up over your face,
show the nations your nakedness
and the kingdoms your disgrace.

I will cast filth upon you
and disgrace you,
and set you up as a gazingstock.

Cush was her strength, and Egypt, without limit;
Put and the Libyans were your helpers.{d}

Your shepherds slumber, O king of Assyria;
your nobles lie still.
Your people are scattered on the mountains,
with no one to gather them.

Nothing can ease your injury;
your wound is fatal.
Everyone who learns of you
applauds your fall.
For who has escaped your endless cruelty?

notes.text: No-amon, “city of Amon,” is Thebes in Upper Egypt. The Assyrians sacked it about 663 BC.
Here “the sea” (yam) means the broad waters of the Nile. “And water her wall” is literally “from the sea her wall.” The Septuagint has “and whose walls are water.”

Cush is the upper Nile region (ancient Nubia). Put was probably in Libya, though some place it on the African coast of the Red Sea. The Hebrew has “your helpers,” but the Septuagint has “her helpers.”
The Hebrew uses several words for locusts (yeleq, ’arbeh, and gov in verse 17). The kinds or stages of locust they refer to are uncertain.
The words translated “guardsmen” (minzarim) and “officials” (tifsarim) are rare. The second may be a loanword from Akkadian, and the precise meaning of both is uncertain.
